People say the rusted swings at this abandoned park still move when there is no wind.
Princeton, West Virginia. Lake Shawnee Amusement Park, Mercer County.

In 1783 this land belonged to settler Mitchell Clay. While he was away, three of his children were attacked here. A daughter and a son were killed, and another son was taken captive. In 1926 Conley Snidow opened an amusement park on the same ground, with a Ferris wheel, a swing ride, a pool and cabins for coal mining families.

Two people drowned in the lake during those years, and in 1966 a young girl was killed on the swing ride. The park closed in 1967, reopened briefly in 1987 and shut for good in 1988. In the early 1990s, work on the property turned up Native American artifacts, and Marshall University archaeologists uncovered thirteen skeletons, mostly elderly people and young children.

The debate: the owners later began running Halloween paranormal tours, and the park has been on Scariest Places on Earth, Ghost Lab and The Dead Files. Skeptics say a few sad accidents over 62 years are not a curse, and some call the tours a business built on graves. Visitors still describe a little girl in a pink dress near the swings.

Would you walk past those swings after dark?

Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Shawnee_Amusement_Park

A TV crew filmed lights pacing their cargo plane over New Zealand, and one of them sat off the wingtip for almost a quarter of an hour.
Kaikoura, New Zealand. Late December 1978.

Top 5 things to know about the Kaikoura lights:

1) It started December 21, 1978, when Safe Air pilots Vern Powell and Ian Pirie saw strange lights around their Argosy cargo plane between Blenheim and Christchurch. Air traffic control radar at Wellington tracked targets at the same time.

2) On the night of December 30, a TV crew from Melbourne's Channel 0, reporter Quentin Fogarty and cameraman David Crockett, rode along on a Safe Air newspaper run to film background for a story about those sightings.

3) The lights came back. Captain Bill Startup called the crew to the flight deck, and for many minutes the people up front watched lights move above, below and in front of the plane. Startup described "a huge, bright white light with a red tinge to it."

4) On the return flight, a line of small lights and a large lighted orb fell in off the wingtip and tracked the plane for almost 15 minutes while it was filmed in color on 16mm. On the tape, Fogarty says, "Let's hope they're friendly."

5) The film made news around the world. Explanations offered over the years include squid fishing boat lights, the planet Venus and reflections, and none has satisfied everyone.

What would you have said if you were on that flight deck?

Learn more: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaikoura_lights

Riders on the Texas frontier swore they saw a wild girl running with a pack of wolves.
Del Rio, Texas, and the Devil's River country. 1835 to 1852.

In 1835 trapper John Dent and his wife Mollie were living in a brush camp on the Devil's River. When her labor went badly, Dent rode for help and was struck dead by lightning. By the time neighbors found the camp, Mollie was dead, wolf tracks were everywhere, and there was no sign of the baby.

In 1845 a boy at San Felipe Springs, now Del Rio, said he saw a creature with long hair that looked like a naked girl, running with lobo wolves that were attacking goats. Later sightings led ranchers to rope her and lock her in a room, where she screamed and howled through the night until wolves answered from the dark. By morning she was gone. In 1852 a survey party said they saw a young woman on a sandbar by the river with two wolf pups. She ran into the brush and was never seen again.

The debate: folklorists say the story was written down decades later and much of it cannot be checked against records. Others point out that families along the Devil's River kept telling it for generations, and some say she is still out there.

Do you think she survived out there?

Source: https://www.texasescapes.com/TexasFolklore/Wolf-Girl-of-Devils-River.htm

An Air Force jet went after an unknown target over New York. Minutes later its crew bailed out and the jet fell on a small town.
Walesville, New York, near Utica. July 2, 1954.

According to records gathered by NICAP researchers, an F-94C Starfire was diverted from a training mission to an active air defense mission near the Griffiss Air Force Base patrol zone. A Pentagon spokesman told reporters the unidentified plane was about 75 miles northeast of Rome when the jets intercepted it. As the jet closed in, the story goes, a sudden, unbearable heat filled the cockpit. The pilot and the radar officer ejected and survived.

The empty jet came down in Walesville, and four people on the ground were killed. Newspapers at the time reported a blaze in the cockpit, and Project Blue Book's own index lists a UFO sighting at Walesville that day, with no evaluation given.

The debate: Major Donald Keyhoe made it famous as a UFO chase gone wrong. Researcher Kevin Randle argued it was an ordinary cockpit fire with no UFO involved. NICAP's Fran Ridge says it is not just a jet crash with a UFO added later.

Would you have pushed in closer?

Source: https://www.nicap.org/540702walesville_dir.htm

"There's a whole fleet of them." A Navy pilot said it on tape while his jet's camera locked onto something rotating over the Atlantic.
Off Jacksonville, Florida. F/A-18 Super Hornets from the USS Theodore Roosevelt, January 2015.

During training off the East Coast, Navy pilots flying from the Roosevelt kept picking up unknown objects on their instruments. One crew's infrared targeting camera recorded a dark oval shape with a glow around it. On the tape you can hear them: "Look at that thing," and "It's rotating," as the object holds against the wind and slowly tips on its side.

Lieutenant Ryan Graves, who flew with that strike group, later told 60 Minutes they were seeing these objects every day for at least a couple of years. The video, nicknamed GIMBAL, was published by The New York Times in December 2017. In April 2020 the Pentagon officially released it and said the objects were still unidentified.

The debate: skeptics such as Mick West argue the "rotation" is the camera's own gimbal turning and the glow is glare from a distant jet engine. Pilots and some analysts say that does not explain the radar returns or the fleet the crew described.

What do you think the camera caught?

Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pentagon_UFO_videos

Only one man was ever hanged in this prison's gallows room, and visitors say something in that cell house never left.
Boise, Idaho. The Old Idaho Penitentiary, in the foothills east of downtown.

The Old Pen held prisoners from 1872 to 1973, more than 13,000 of them, including Harry Orchard, who assassinated former Governor Frank Steunenberg, and Lyda Southard, the woman newspapers called Idaho's Lady Bluebeard. Riots over living conditions broke out in 1952, 1971 and 1973, and after the last one burned several buildings, the prison closed that December.

In 1957 Raymond Snowden was hanged in the gallows room of the maximum security cell house, the only execution ever carried out there. Visitors and paranormal teams, including Ghost Adventures, describe voices, being physically touched, and a heavy, strange feeling, most of all in the gallows room and in the solitary confinement cells known as Siberia. Ghost lore also talks about cell doors moving on their own and gasping sounds in the dark.

The debate: the Idaho State Historical Society, which runs the site, says there is no conclusive evidence of ghosts and leaves it to each visitor to decide. It also points out that only Snowden died in the gallows room, even though many retellings claim more hangings there. Its night investigations still sell out.

Would you spend a night in Siberia?

Source: https://history.idaho.gov/oldpen/

Tower operators watched a dark shape with a light on it maneuver over Tokyo for almost an hour, and the Air Force filed it as an Unknown.
Tokyo, Japan. Haneda Air Force Base, about 11:30 PM, August 5, 1952.

Top 5 things to know about the Haneda UFO case:

1) The tower: controllers at Haneda, on the edge of Tokyo Bay, spotted a bright light and, through binoculars, a darker shape behind it. They watched it for 50 to 60 minutes as it hovered, flew curves and moved as fast as about 330 knots.

2) The radar: ground radar picked up the target, and at one point the single return seemed to split into three.

3) The intercept: an F-94 Starfire crew, 1st Lt. W. R. Holder and 1st Lt. A. M. Jones, was sent up. Their airborne radar locked on for about 90 seconds before the target pulled away.

4) The verdict: the Air Force listed Haneda as an Unknown, and Blue Book chief Captain Edward Ruppelt later wrote about it as one of the cases that impressed his sources most.

5) The timing: it came at the peak of the summer 1952 UFO wave, about a week after radar targets over Washington, D.C. made front pages. NICAP researchers still rank it among the most important radar cases on record.

Would you trust the tower crew, the radar or the pilots?

Learn more: https://www.nicap.org/520805haneda_dir.htm

He filmed two spinning silver objects in broad daylight, and when the Air Force sent the film back, he said the best frames were missing.
Great Falls, Montana. Legion Stadium, 11:29 AM, August 15, 1950.

Nick Mariana, general manager of the Great Falls Electrics minor league baseball team, was checking the field with his 19 year old secretary, Virginia Raunig, when a bright flash caught his eye. Two bright, silvery, rotating objects were crossing the sky over the city. He ran to his car, grabbed his 16mm color movie camera and filmed them for 16 seconds. Raunig saw them too.

The Air Force sent the film to Wright-Patterson and returned it with a letter saying its analysts found nothing unusual. Mariana said the first 35 frames, the ones that showed spinning discs most clearly, had been removed. The Air Force said it took out only a single damaged frame.

The debate: the first answer was sunlight glinting off two F-94 jets known to be in the area. In 1952 Blue Book studied the film again, ruled out the jets, and Captain Edward Ruppelt called it an unknown. In 1953 the CIA backed Robertson Panel decided it was aircraft reflections after all. It remains one of the earliest UFO films ever shot.

Would you have handed your film to the Air Force?

Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mariana_UFO_film

A radar on the ground and the radar inside a fighter jet both locked onto the same light over South Dakota.
Rapid City, South Dakota. Ellsworth Air Force Base, the night of August 5, 1953.

Just after 9 PM, a Ground Observer Corps volunteer in Black Hawk, about 8 miles northwest of Rapid City, called Ellsworth about a bright red light low over the hills. It raced off toward Rapid City, turning greener as it picked up speed, then came back. Radar at the base found targets, and airmen sent outside saw a fast light heading south.

An F-84 was vectored in and the pilot made visual contact before the target moved out to 70 miles. A second F-84 climbed to 15,000 feet and watched a light much brighter than a star jump in elevation and change from white to green. His radar gunsight showed a target out ahead, and ground radar tracked it 5 to 10 miles in front of the jet for 80 miles before it went off the scope. The radar scope photos and gun camera film reportedly malfunctioned.

The debate: Project Blue Book never put it on its list of Unknowns, but its own case papers called it unsolved, and Captain Edward Ruppelt featured it in his book as one of the strongest radar and visual cases. Skeptics say bright stars and ground clutter can fool both eyes and radar.

Would you trust a radar lock, two pilots and a ground spotter all at once?

Source: https://www.nicap.org/530805ellsworth_dir.htm

"It's not an aircraft." Those were the last words a 20 year old pilot radioed before he vanished over the sea.
Melbourne, Australia. A Cessna 182 bound for King Island, over Bass Strait near Cape Otway, about 7:06 PM, October 21, 1978.

Frederick Valentich had about 150 hours of flying time when he called Melbourne Flight Service to ask about a large aircraft following him at 4,500 feet. There was no known traffic. He said it had four bright lights, passed about 1,000 feet overhead at high speed, and seemed to be "orbiting" above him with a shiny metal surface and a green light. Then he reported his engine was running rough.

At 7:12 PM he said, "It's not an aircraft." His microphone stayed open for 17 seconds of a metallic scraping noise, and then nothing. A sea and air search covering more than 1,000 square miles found no trace. Five years later an engine cowl flap from the same model of Cessna washed up on Flinders Island.

The debate: Department of Transport officials suggested he became disoriented and saw his own lights reflected in the water while flying upside down. Others think he staged his own disappearance. Skeptics point to a meteor stream that night, while ufologists point to people who said they saw an erratic green light in the sky.

What do you think was above him?

Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disappearance_of_Frederick_Valentich

They say a bloodstain on the stairs of this old house will not scrub out, and the young officer who died on those steps was buried standing up, facing England.
Beaufort, North Carolina. The Hammock House, on a low rise near Taylor Creek.

The Hammock House is named for the old word for a low hill, a rise so noticeable that ships coming in from the sea once used it as a landmark. The story goes that it was an inn in Beaufort's busy colonial port days, and that a wealthy captain with a fierce temper, known as "Mad" Brothers, sailed home the night of a farewell dance there. He burst into the ballroom, saw his bride to be dancing in the arms of a British naval lieutenant, and drew his sword. He chased the man up the stairs and stabbed him through the heart. Only then did he learn the lieutenant was her brother. Visitors still describe a dark stain on the steps, and the legend points to an upright grave in Beaufort's Old Burying Ground. Locals add that Blackbeard himself stayed at the inn.

The debate: some local historians date the house to around 1800, decades after Blackbeard died in 1718, and no record has ever confirmed the duel or the names in the story. Believers say the stairs speak for themselves.

Would you walk up those stairs at night?

Source: https://northcarolinaghosts.com/coast/the-duel-at-hammock-house/

For more than 40 years, glowing balls of light have floated through one small valley in Norway, and scientists with a full time monitoring station still cannot tell you what they are.
Hessdalen, Norway. A 7.5 mile valley in rural central Norway.

Top 5 things to know about the Hessdalen lights:

1) Where it happens: the Hessdalen valley in central Norway, where unexplained lights have been reported since at least the 1930s. They show up day and night, usually white, yellow or red, above and below the horizon.

2) The peak: from December 1981 to mid 1984, the lights appeared 15 to 20 times a week. Overnight tourists packed the valley to see them hover, sway slowly, or race off at enormous speed.

3) Project Hessdalen: in 1983 Norwegian and Swedish researchers hauled cameras, radar and instruments into the snow. Their 1984 report admitted they had not found out what the phenomenon was, only that it could be measured.

4) The station: since 1998 an automatic measurement station has watched the valley around the clock, with scientists from Ostfold University College and Italy's National Research Council studying the recordings.

5) The theories: burning dust from local mining, glowing plasma from radon decay, charged rocks under strain, even a valley acting like a natural battery. None of them explains everything, and there is still no consensus.

Would you spend a night in that valley to see them for yourself?

Learn more: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hessdalen_lights

A police officer radioed that he was looking at a UFO. Then a blue flash killed his squad car, his headlights and his radio.
Elmwood, Wisconsin. Tuttle Hill above a limestone quarry, about 11:00 PM, April 22, 1976.

Relief officer George Wheeler, a 30 year police veteran and World War II combat pilot, drove up Tuttle Hill thinking an orange glow was a fire. Instead he found a silver craft hovering about 100 feet off the ground, with six bluish white portholes along its side, shadows moving inside, and a top glowing so bright it was "like looking into the sun." He radioed the sheriff's office in Ellsworth. The object shot straight up with a whoosh and a blue flash, and his car went dead.

Dairy farmer David Moots found him dazed, trying to get out of the car. Wheeler told him he had been hit. "Hit by a car?" "No, one of those UFOs." A woman north of town saw a bright orange, moon shaped object on the same hill at 11 o'clock, and a neighboring farmer said his TV cut out a few minutes after 11.

The debate: Wheeler had reported a sighting the year before, and researchers like J. Allen Hynek were wary of repeat witnesses. But investigators Robert Pratt and University of Wisconsin River Falls biology professor Jack Bostrak found other witnesses who backed up the glow. Elmwood never forgot that night.

Would you have driven up that hill?

Source: http://www.ufoevidence.org/cases/case341.htm

Three glowing objects paced an airliner full of passengers across Pennsylvania for 45 minutes, and at least two other airline crews saw them too.
Williamsport, Pennsylvania. An American Airlines DC-6B from Newark to Detroit, about 8:20 PM, February 24, 1959.

Captain Peter Killian and First Officer James Dee were at 8,500 feet on a clear, moonless night when Killian noticed three bright lights off the left wingtip. He first took them for the belt of Orion, then saw Orion higher overhead. The lights flared "brighter than any star," faded out completely, shifted from yellow orange to a brilliant blue white, and the last one in line kept moving back and forth on its own.

Near Erie, Killian radioed two other American Airlines planes, and both crews found the objects to the south. Over Ohio, a United Airlines crew said three lights paced them for half an hour from near Lock Haven to Youngstown, and ground observers around Akron phoned in nine reports of three UFOs heading west.

The debate: the Air Force said the pilots saw a KC-97 tanker refueling three B-47 bombers near Bradford, Pennsylvania. NICAP pointed out that Bradford is north of the flight path, while every crew saw the lights to the south. Killian never accepted the explanation.

Would you trust three airline crews or the tanker explanation?

Source: http://www.nicap.org/reports/590224williamsport_report1.htm

A weather radar operator watched something shoot thousands of feet straight up, and a police officer on the ground saw it do the same thing at the same moment.
Holland, Michigan. Ottawa County on the Lake Michigan shore, the night of March 8, 1994.

Calls about strange lights were pouring into the Ottawa County dispatch center, more than 100 witnesses by the end of the night. With no aircraft to blame, the dispatcher phoned the National Weather Service office in Muskegon and asked if anything was showing up on radar.

Meteorologist Jack Bushong was working alone. There were no thunderstorms to track, so he took the radar off automatic and swept the beam across the county by hand. He found a single strong return coasting at about 100 mph. It stopped, hovered, then climbed to 5,000 feet, then 10,000, while an officer on the line reported the same object doing the same thing. Soon there were three of them, roughly 20 miles apart, one on the lakeshore, jumping position faster than he could describe them. The call was recorded.

The debate: there is still no accepted explanation for the returns. Bushong, who spent his whole career reading weather radar, says the targets moved faster than he could describe them. The case was later featured on Unsolved Mysteries.

Would you have believed the radar or your own eyes?

Source: https://wwmt.com/news/local/retired-meteorologist-shares-his-account-of-1994-west-michigan-ufo-sightings

A young bride waited in Room 501 of a grand beach hotel for a ship that never came, and guests say she is still watching the Gulf from the turret.
Galveston, Texas. The Hotel Galvez on Seawall Boulevard, opened in 1911.

The Galvez went up on the new seawall a decade after the 1900 hurricane killed about 6,000 people in Galveston, and it became the island's grand beachfront address. Gamblers, movie stars and presidents stayed there, and during World War II the Coast Guard took it over. Since the 1950s, guests have reported ghosts, especially on the fifth floor.

The best known is Audra, the "Lovelorn Lady." The story says that in the mid 1950s a young bride to be checked into Room 501 to wait for her fiancé, a sailor, and climbed to the hotel's west turret every day to watch for his ship. After a storm she was told it had gone down with all hands, and in her grief she hanged herself in the turret. Days later, the legend says, he arrived in Galveston alive. Guests in 501 describe doors slamming, lights and TVs switching on, phones ringing with no one on the line, key cards that will not work, and a woman crying near the fifth floor elevators.

The debate: no record has ever been found that confirms who Audra was or that she died there, and the hotel runs its own ghost tours. Historians call her folklore. Guests who stayed in 501 are not so sure.

Would you book Room 501?

Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hotel_Galvez

For five months, thousands of people across Belgium said a giant black triangle was floating silently over their towns, and one night the Air Force sent two F-16 fighters after it.
Eupen, Belgium. November 29, 1989 to April 1990.

Top 5 things to know about the Belgian UFO wave:

1) Where it started: the first big night was November 29, 1989, around Eupen, near the German border. 143 people reported seeing something, and by the end of the wave thousands claimed sightings.

2) The shape: most witnesses described a large, flat triangle flying low and slow with bright lights underneath, often with no sound at all.

3) The scramble: on the night of March 30, 1990, ground radar tracked an unknown target and two Belgian Air Force F-16s were sent up to find it. The pilots never saw it with their own eyes, but the Air Force released a report on the night, and the case is still argued over today.

4) The photo: in April 1990 a picture of a black triangle with lights at its corners, taken near Petit-Rechain, went around the world. Experts could not prove it fake for 20 years. In 2011, the photographer admitted it was a polystyrene model with lightbulbs.

5) The explanations: skeptics point to helicopters, media hype and the fact that many reports came in after the news coverage. Belgium's air staff suspected secret American stealth planes, but the U.S. said none were flying there.

Which is stranger: thousands of witnesses, or radar that saw what the pilots couldn't?

Learn more: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belgian_UFO_wave

A Homeland Security patrol plane's heat camera locked onto something racing across an airport in the dark, and then it dove into the ocean and came back out as two.
Aguadilla, Puerto Rico. Rafael Hernández Airport, the old Ramey Air Force Base, about 9:22 PM, April 25, 2013.

A U.S. Customs and Border Protection Dash 8 patrol plane was flying near the airport when its infrared camera picked up a small, warm object with no lights. The crew kept the camera on it for about three minutes as it crossed the runway area, skimmed low over houses and trees, and headed out over the beach. Then it appeared to plunge into the Atlantic, come back up, and split into two objects before the footage ended.

In 2015, a team from the Scientific Coalition for UAP Studies went through the video frame by frame and said the object flew below treetop level at up to about 100 mph through an urban area without hitting anything, then entered the water with almost no splash.

The debate: in March 2025 the Pentagon's UFO office, AARO, closed the case. It said the objects were most likely a pair of sky lanterns drifting on the wind, which hotels near the beach often release, and that the "dive" was just the lanterns cooling until the camera could no longer see them. Researchers still argue about the speed and the split.

Sky lanterns, or something that can fly into the sea and come back out?

Police officers in five small Illinois towns watched the same huge lighted object glide over them before dawn, and one of them ran to his trunk for a camera.
Lebanon, Illinois. St. Clair County, east of St. Louis, about 4:10 AM, January 5, 2000.

It started when a man walked into the Highland police station and asked an officer to come outside and look at something hovering in the sky. The call went out over the county radio. In Lebanon, Officer Ed Barton looked southeast and saw two extremely bright white lights hanging in the sky, part of a much larger dark shape. Officers in Shiloh, Millstadt and Dupo heard the traffic and went looking too. In Millstadt, Officer Craig Stevens watched it pass at about 4:28, grabbed the Polaroid from his squad car's trunk, and got one blurry picture in the 15 degree cold before it slipped away to the northwest.

Witnesses described something as big as a football field, flat or triangular, with bright white lights and red lights at the rear, moving slowly and silently, then speeding off. Its path ran about two miles from Scott Air Force Base, which said it had no aircraft like that in the air and did not track anything on radar.

The debate: the officers' descriptions do not match perfectly, and skeptics say lights seen at night from different angles are easy to misjudge. But five officers in five towns were on the radio about the same thing at the same time.

If five officers saw it, why does nobody know what it was?

Source: http://www.ufoevidence.org/cases/case277.htm

The man who would design the U-2 and SR-71 spy planes watched a black saucer hang over the Pacific for three minutes, while his own test pilots chased it at 17,000 feet.
Agoura, California. A hilltop ranch three miles west of Agoura, about 5:00 PM, December 16, 1953.

Clarence "Kelly" Johnson, chief engineer at Lockheed, was watching the sunset through his ranch house window when he noticed a dark object above the mountains to the west. He thought it was a smoke trail or a lenticular cloud, but its sharp outline never changed and it did not move for at least three minutes. He sent his wife for the binoculars, ran outside, and watched the long, thin ellipse speed off to the west in a shallow climb. Within 90 seconds it was gone. He placed it roughly over Point Mugu.

At the same time, a Lockheed crew was flying a Navy Super Constellation test flight off the coast. Test pilot Roy Wimmer called out "Look out, there's a flying saucer," and co-pilot Rudy Thoren turned straight toward a dark, sharp edged object that looked like a giant flying wing. They flew at it for about five minutes at some 225 mph and never gained on it. Then it shrank to a speck and vanished, heading west. The next morning, before Thoren could say where or when, Johnson told him.

The debate: Project Blue Book filed it as a lenticular cloud. Johnson wrote that he was "more firmly convinced than ever" such craft exist, and an Air Force general noted he had been reluctant to write the report at all. The Pentagon released the full file on November 20, 2026.

If the best aircraft designer of his era couldn't explain it, who could?

For 168 years this prison held killers, bank robbers and a future heavyweight champion, and the guides who lead night tours there now say some of the prisoners never left.
Jefferson City, Missouri. The Missouri State Penitentiary on the bluffs of the Missouri River, opened in 1836 and closed in 2004.

When it shut down, it was the oldest operating prison west of the Mississippi. Sonny Liston learned to box inside its walls, Pretty Boy Floyd and Emma Goldman did time there, and in 1967 James Earl Ray escaped hidden in a bread box on a delivery truck, a year before he killed Martin Luther King Jr. A riot in 1954 left four inmates dead, dozens hurt and buildings burned, and from 1938 to 1965 the state put 39 people to death in the small stone gas chamber that still stands on the grounds.

Since the prison opened for tours, guides and guests have described footsteps on empty walkways, cell doors moving on their own, shadow figures in the old 1868 A-Hall, and voices in the underground dungeon cells. Guides tell visitors that blondes and redheads are the ones most likely to be touched, and some guests say it happened to them. Ghost Hunters and Ghost Adventures have both filmed there.

The debate: the site sells ghost tours by the night, so the stories are good for business, and an old stone cellblock full of drafts, echoes and steel doors will always sound like someone is walking right behind you.

Would you sign up for the five hour ghost tour?

Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Missouri_State_Penitentiary

A radio telescope in Ohio caught a signal from deep space so strong that the volunteer reading the printout circled it in red and wrote one word in the margin: "Wow!"
Delaware, Ohio. Ohio State University's Big Ear radio telescope, 10:16 PM Eastern, August 15, 1977.

Top 5 things to know about the Wow! signal:

1) The telescope: Big Ear was a huge open air radio telescope near Perkins Observatory in Delaware, Ohio, and from 1973 it ran the longest search for alien radio signals in history.

2) The note: a few days after the signal hit, volunteer astronomer Jerry Ehman was going through the computer printouts when he saw the string 6EQUJ5, circled it and wrote "Wow!" beside it. Those characters measure how loud the signal was over time. They are not a coded message.

3) The channel: it came from the direction of the constellation Sagittarius, very close to 1420 megahertz, the natural radio frequency of hydrogen. Back in 1959 two physicists had picked that frequency as the most likely channel an alien civilization would use to call.

4) Seventy two seconds: as the Earth turned, Big Ear could watch one point in the sky for about 72 seconds, and the signal rose and fell across that whole window, just like something fixed out in space. The telescope had two receiver horns, and the signal should have shown up in the second one about three minutes later. It never did.

5) It never came back: Ehman and later teams pointed telescopes at that patch of sky more than 100 times. Nothing. Explanations include an Earth signal bouncing off space junk, hydrogen around passing comets, and a natural flare from a cloud of hydrogen gas. None has been confirmed.

If it was a message, why did it only knock once?

Learn more: https://www.bigear.org/wow.htm

A farm wife walking home from feeding her rabbits saw a silver disc gliding silently over the field, and her husband grabbed the camera and took two of the most famous UFO photos ever made.
McMinnville, Oregon. The Trent farm near Sheridan, about 13 miles southwest of McMinnville, about 7:30 PM, May 11, 1950.

Evelyn Trent called to her husband Paul, who ran for the family's loaded Kodak and snapped two pictures of the slow, metallic, disc shaped object before it sped off to the west. Paul's father said he saw it too. The Trents later said they thought it might be a secret military plane and worried the pictures would bring trouble, so they did not rush to show anyone. A local banker put the prints in his window, the McMinnville Telephone-Register ran them on the front page on June 8, and Life magazine printed them weeks later.

In 1967, astronomer William K. Hartmann of the Air Force funded Condon Committee studied the negatives and interviewed the Trents. He wrote that this was one of the few UFO reports where everything he checked appeared consistent with an extraordinary, silvery, metallic, disc shaped flying object, tens of meters across. He also admitted it could be a small model hanging from a wire.

The debate: skeptics Philip Klass and Robert Sheaffer called it a hoax, pointing to shadows that look like morning rather than evening and a shape that resembles an old car mirror. In 2013 a French research group said it could see a thread above the object. Evelyn and Paul Trent insisted it was real until they died in the 1990s, and McMinnville now throws one of the biggest UFO festivals in the country every spring.

Do those two photos show a real craft or a model on a string?

Source: https://www.nicap.org/500511mcminnville_dir.htm

A glowing object shaped like a mushroom hovered over a Kansas sheep farm, and when it shot away it left a glowing ring on the ground that went numb under a woman's fingers.
Delphos, Kansas. The Johnson family farm in Ottawa County, about 7 PM, November 2, 1971.

Sixteen year old Ronald Johnson was doing chores near the sheep pen with the farm dog, Snowball, when he heard a rumble like a washing machine out of balance. About 75 feet away, an object shaped like a toadstool, about 8 feet across, hung 2 to 5 feet above the ground with a shimmering glow running from its base down to the dirt. When it tilted and shot away with a high whine like a jet, Ronald was briefly blinded. His parents, Durel and Erma, ran outside in time to see a light in the sky and a glowing ring on the ground. When Erma touched it, her fingertips went numb.

The next day, reporter Thaddia Smith of the Delphos Republican called the Ottawa County Sheriff. Undersheriff Harlan Enlow found a doughnut shaped ring of bone dry soil in a yard that was otherwise mud, with broken limbs on the trees nearby. They had to force Snowball back to the spot, where he shivered and pawed the ground. Weeks later, investigator Ted Phillips found the soil in the ring still dry about a foot down and the ring outlined in snow that would not melt.

The debate: doubters have blamed a fungus ring or a hoax, but the sheriff's office saw the ring the next day and the family told the same story for the rest of their lives.

What could leave a ring of soil that water would not soak into?

Source: https://www.nicap.org/ar-711102rep.htm

Two airline pilots watched eight glowing red discs race in under their plane and flip around in a hairpin turn "like balls bouncing off a wall."
Norfolk, Virginia. Over the Chesapeake Bay, 20 to 25 miles north of Norfolk, 9:12 PM, July 14, 1952.

Pan American First Officer William B. Nash and Second Officer William H. Fortenberry were flying a DC-4 airliner at 8,000 feet on a clear night when they saw a red glow on the ground ahead, near Newport News. It turned into six round, flat objects shaped like coins, each about 100 feet across, glowing a fiery red and flying in a tight line about 2,000 feet above the bay. Almost directly under the airliner, all six stopped short and reversed direction in a sharp 150 degree turn. Two more, brighter than the rest, came up from behind the plane and joined them. Then all eight blinked out together, lit back up, and climbed as a group toward Newport News before winking out one by one.

The debate: ground witnesses reported similar lights that night, the Air Force questioned both pilots, and Project Blue Book filed the case as an unknown. Later skeptics blamed ground lights seen through haze, fireflies trapped between the cockpit window panes, and even a mirage of the planet Venus.

Could two veteran airline pilots really mistake fireflies for eight discs?

Source: https://www.nicap.org/520714norfolk_dir.htm
